transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I... I honestly don't even know where to start. It’s just... it’s all too much right now. I’ve always been the one who fixes things, you know? I’m a heavy equipment mechanic, I work on massive diesel rigs and loaders, so I'm used to handling pressure and getting my hands dirty. But lately, ever since those foreclosure notices started coming in the mail... I just feel like I’m completely coming apart at the seams. 

I mean, it’s honestly embarrassing. I’m a forty-seven-year-old woman and I’m sitting out in the cab of my truck in the lot before my shift, just bawling my eyes out. I have to sit there for twenty minutes wiping my face just to pull myself together enough to walk into the shop. And even then, I'm just a wreck all day. I’m jumping out of my skin every single time my cell phone rings because I’m terrified it’s the bank or a collection agency calling again. 

And it’s really bleeding into my work, which is dangerous with the kind of machinery I handle. I've been snapping at the new apprentices over absolutely nothing—and I'm usually the one who likes teaching them and cutting them some slack! But worse than that, I’m out there in the repair bay making these stupid, careless mistakes. I'm missing obvious things on the inspection sheets, torquing things wrong... mistakes I never, ever would have made before all this bank stuff started. I've been doing this job a long time and I'm good at it, but right now I just can't seem to get my head straight, and I just... I don't know how to stop it.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed feeling down, hopeless, or have you lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Well, it's... it's not exactly that I feel hopeless, you know? Like, I don't wake up thinking the world is ending or that there's no point to anything. It's more just this constant, crushing weight of the situation. I mean, I still care about things. I still want to fix my truck, I still want to go to the lake on weekends like I used to, but... I just can't seem to find the energy or the focus to actually do them. 

Like, last weekend, I was supposed to go fishing with my brother. We've been planning this trip for months, right? And usually, I'd be out there prepping the gear, checking the lines, getting everything ready days in advance. But this time... I just sat on the couch staring at the wall. I couldn't even bring myself to pack a cooler. It's not that I didn't want to go, it's just that my brain is so wrapped up in all this financial mess that there's no room left for anything else. 

And as for feeling down... I guess I do, but it's more of an anxious, frantic kind of down. It's not this deep, dark sadness, it's more like... like I'm drowning, and I can see the surface, but I just can't reach it. I'm just so overwhelmed by the bank stuff, the calls, the letters... it's like a dark cloud hanging over me all the time. But I don't think it's hopelessness, exactly. I just... I just want it to stop, you know? I want my life back.
Do you find yourself worrying about a lot of different things, even when there isn't an immediate problem, or does your anxiety mostly center around your financial situation?

Well, it's... it's definitely the money. I mean, the house, the bank, the foreclosure... that's the whole thing. Before all this started happening, I wasn't really a worrier. I mean, sure, I'd worry about normal things, like if a repair on a loader was going to take longer than we quoted, or if my old truck was going to pass inspection, but that's just normal life stuff, right? You fix it and you move on. I never used to just sit around spinning my wheels about what-ifs. 

But now... it's like this financial thing is this massive black hole, and it's just sucking everything else into it. I mean, I'm not sitting there worrying about getting sick, or the economy, or the weather, or anything like that. It's just... the house. The letters. Every time the mail carrier pulls up to the box, my stomach just drops into my shoes. I literally watch them out the window, and I start sweating, thinking, "Is today the day they tell me I have thirty days to get out?" 

And then I start thinking about where I'm going to put all my tools if I lose the house, because I have this huge rolling chest, right? It's a Snap-on, I've been building that collection for twenty years, and it won't just fit in some tiny apartment. And if I can't keep my tools safe, how am I going to do my job? So it all comes back to the money and the house. It's just this one huge, glaring problem that I can't fix, no matter how hard I try to wrench on it. I just keep replaying conversations with the bank in my head, thinking of what I should have said, or what I'm going to say if they call again... it's exhausting, but it's really just focused on this one giant mess.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms like restlessness, trouble sleeping, or muscle tension lately?

Physical symptoms? Well... I mean, I guess I haven't really thought about it like that, because I'm just so focused on the bank stuff, you know? Like, I haven't really noticed my muscles being tense or anything. I mean, my job is physical, so I'm always a little sore. I'm wrestling with these massive tires and pulling heavy transmissions all day, so my back and shoulders always ache, but that's just the job, right? That's not new. I haven't noticed any extra tension or anything like that.

And as for sleeping... honestly, I don't think my sleep is any worse than usual. I mean, I've always been a bit of a light sleeper, ever since I started working the early shift years ago. I get up at 4:30 AM, so I'm usually pretty wiped out by the time I get home, take a shower, and try to scrub all the grease off my hands. Sometimes I have a hard time falling asleep right away, but that's just because my brain is going, you know? But I wouldn't say I'm having trouble sleeping, not really. I'm not tossing and turning all night or waking up at 2 AM staring at the ceiling. 

And restlessness... I don't know. I mean, I'm pacing around a lot when I'm on the phone with the mortgage company, but who wouldn't? You're on hold for forty-five minutes listening to that terrible elevator music, waiting for someone to tell you if you're going to lose your home. Of course I'm pacing! But it's not like I'm just sitting on the couch and my legs won't stop bouncing for no reason. It's all just... it's all tied to the house. Everything is just tied to the house. So, yeah, I haven't really noticed any of those physical things you mentioned. Just the crying in the truck and the mistakes at work, really.
Have you ever had sudden episodes where your heart races, you feel short of breath, or you’re afraid something terrible is going to happen right then and there?

Sudden episodes? Like... like a panic attack or something? No, no, I haven't had anything like that. I mean, my heart definitely beats faster when I'm opening a letter from the bank, but that's just because I'm terrified of what it's going to say, you know? It's not like it just happens out of the blue while I'm, I don't know, grocery shopping or watching TV. 

I don't get short of breath, either. I mean, the only time I'm breathing hard is if I'm trying to break loose a rusted lug nut on a dual-wheel axle that hasn't been off in five years. You really have to put your whole back into it, maybe even get a cheater bar, and yeah, you're going to be huffing and puffing after that. But just sitting there, feeling like I can't breathe? No, nothing like that. 

And that feeling of something terrible happening right then and there... well, like I said, the terrible thing is the foreclosure. It's not a sudden fear, it's just this constant, looming dread. It's like I know the terrible thing is coming, but it's a slow-moving train wreck. It's not like I'm suddenly terrified I'm having a heart attack or something. It's always just the house, the bank, the money. It's never just this random, out-of-control panic. It's all very specific to my situation, you know? So, no, I wouldn't say I've had any of those sudden episodes you're talking about.
Have you found that things you used to enjoy, like fixing your truck or going to the lake, don’t give you any pleasure anymore?

Well, I mean... I still like fixing things. I still like the truck. It's just... it's hard to explain. It's not that I don't get any pleasure out of it anymore, it's more like I just don't have the time or the energy to even think about it right now. I mean, my old Ford, she needs a new alternator, and usually, that's the kind of weekend project I'd look forward to. I'd grab a couple of beers, pull her into the driveway, get under the hood, and just tinker. It's peaceful, you know? Just me and the engine. But lately, every time I look at the truck, all I can think about is how much the parts are going to cost, and whether I should be spending that money on the mortgage instead. 

And the lake... gosh, I used to love going out to the lake. We have this little spot we've been going to for years, just a quiet cove where you can cast a line and not hear a single car on the highway. But I haven't been out there in months. It's not that I wouldn't enjoy it if I went, I just... I can't justify it. How can I sit out there on a lawn chair, watching a bobber float on the water, when I know the bank is probably drafting another letter right at that exact second? I'd just be sitting there, staring at the water, thinking about foreclosure. 

So it's not that the joy is gone from those things, it's just that the worry about the house is so loud, it drowns everything else out. If I could just fix this bank situation, I know I'd be right back under the hood of that Ford, happy as a clam. But right now, there's just no room in my brain for anything else. It's all just consumed by the money and the house. Every single waking minute.
Have you felt down or experienced a loss of interest in activities, even when things weren't actively reminding you of the financial situation?

No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, it's like I was just saying about the truck and the lake, you know? It's not like I'm just walking around in a fog, feeling depressed for no reason. If I'm feeling down, if I'm crying in the cab of my truck on my lunch break, it's because I'm thinking about the bank. It's because I'm thinking about my kids having to pack up their rooms. 

It's never just... disconnected, I guess? Like, I don't wake up on a Saturday morning, look out the window at a beautiful sunny day, and just feel sad for no reason. If I wake up feeling heavy, it's because the first thought in my head is, "Did the mail run yet? Is there a letter?" 

And as for losing interest when I'm not reminded of the money... well, the thing is, I'm *always* reminded of it. It's not like I can just turn it off. I'll be at work, elbow-deep in grease, trying to rebuild a diesel injector, and my mind will just drift right back to the mortgage. Or I'll be at the grocery store, trying to figure out if I can afford the name-brand cereal for the kids, and boom, I'm right back in it. So there really isn't a time when I'm *not* being actively reminded of the financial situation. It's like this heavy backpack I'm wearing every single second of the day. 

But if you're asking if I've ever felt this way before all this bank stuff started, like, just down in the dumps and not wanting to do anything? No. Never. I've always been a doer, you know? I work hard, I play hard. I love my job, even when it wrecks my back. I love my weekends. This whole... whatever this is, this crying and making mistakes and feeling like the sky is falling... it's all 100% because of the house. If the house was safe, I'd be perfectly fine. I know I would.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately, like eating a lot less or a lot more than usual?

Changes in my appetite? Well, I mean, I guess I haven't really been eating the way I normally do, but it's not like I'm starving myself on purpose or anything. It's just... I don't know, my stomach has been in absolute knots for weeks now. 

You know how it is when you're working in the shop all day. Usually, by the time noon rolls around, I am absolutely famished. I'm talking, I could eat a horse. I'd usually pack a big lunch—a couple of thick ham and cheese sandwiches, maybe some potato salad, an apple, a whole thermos of coffee. You need that kind of fuel when you're wrestling with big rig tires and pulling transmissions, you know? It's heavy, physical work. But lately... gosh, lately I just open my lunch cooler and look at it, and the thought of chewing and swallowing just makes me feel a little sick. 

It's like my throat just closes up. I'll take a bite of a sandwich, and it just tastes like sawdust. I just end up chewing it forever, and then I have to wash it down with water just to get it past my throat. So, most days, I end up just tossing half of it in the trash, which kills me because I hate wasting food, especially now with money being so tight. 

And dinners aren't much better. I try to cook for the kids, you know, make sure they have a hot meal—spaghetti, meatloaf, whatever I can throw together after a ten-hour shift. I'll sit down at the table with them, and I'll put food on my plate so they don't worry, but I just end up pushing the peas around with my fork. My youngest, he even asked me the other night, "Mom, aren't you hungry?" And I just had to lie and say I had a big late lunch at work. 

But I haven't really weighed myself or anything. I don't own a scale. I mean, maybe my work pants are fitting a little looser around the waist? I had to pull my belt in an extra notch the other morning, but I don't know if that's because I'm actually losing weight or if the denim is just stretching out, you know how those heavy work jeans get when they're old. 

So, I wouldn't say I'm eating a lot more, definitely not. If anything, I'm eating less, but it's just because I'm so wound up about the house. It's hard to have an appetite when you feel like you've got a cinder block sitting in the bottom of your stomach all day long. If I could just get a letter from the bank saying everything is fine, I swear, I'd go out and eat a 16-ounce ribeye right then and there. But right now? Food just doesn't even appeal to me.
Have you found yourself feeling guilty or blaming yourself for the financial situation, even when it’s not entirely your fault?

Guilty? No... no, I wouldn't say I feel guilty. I mean, I don't blame myself for this, because I know I didn't do anything wrong. It's not like I went out and blew my paycheck on fancy clothes or a new truck or, I don't know, gambling or something. I work hard. I've been at the depot turning wrenches on those heavy rigs for years, and I take every single hour of overtime the foreman will give me. If there's a front-end loader that needs a hydraulic pump replaced on a Friday afternoon, I'm the one staying late to do it, tearing up my knuckles to get it done. I've always paid my bills on time. Always. 

The thing is, they sold my mortgage. The original local bank I was with, they sold it to some massive servicing company out of state, and suddenly there was this huge shortage in my escrow account because they said the county property taxes were recalculated. Next thing I know, I get a letter saying my monthly payment is shooting up by almost six hundred dollars. Six hundred! Who just has an extra six hundred dollars lying around every month? Especially with the price of groceries right now. 

So, no, I don't sit around blaming myself. I did everything you're supposed to do in this life. I went to school, got my ASE certifications, got a good, honest, back-breaking job. I budget every single penny. I sit at the kitchen table every Sunday with my calculator, my grease-stained pay stubs, and a stack of envelopes, and I stretch every dollar until it screams. I even started cutting my own hair just to save the twenty bucks, and I buy the cheapest store-brand everything for myself so the kids can have the good stuff. 

If it was my fault, if I had been reckless or stupid with my money, then yeah, I'd feel guilty. I'd be kicking myself up and down the street. But I didn't cause this. It's just the system, or the bank, or the county taxes... I don't even know who to be mad at half the time. I just feel angry, and mostly just... terrified. I'm terrified they're going to take the house from my kids. But guilt? No. I just feel completely helpless because it's a problem I can't fix. Give me a busted diesel engine, give me a blown transmission, and I'll find the problem and fix it. I know how things fit together. But this? I can't put a wrench to a bank error. I can't rebuild a mortgage. I just have to sit here and wait for the sky to fall, and that's what's driving me absolutely out of my mind.
Have you noticed any trouble concentrating or thinking clearly lately, like it's harder to focus on tasks or make decisions?

Trouble concentrating? I mean... no, I wouldn't say that. It's not like my brain has stopped working or I can't figure things out. I'm not confused or anything like that. 

Like, just yesterday, they brought in this older Peterbilt, right? The driver was complaining about a massive loss of power whenever he was hauling a full load up a grade. Now, some of the younger guys in the shop, they'll just look at the scanner, see a low boost code, and immediately want to throw a brand new turbocharger at it. That's a three-thousand-dollar guess. But I can still think clearly enough to know you don't start there. I made the decision to pull out the pressure tester, hooked it up to the charge air cooler, and sure enough, I found this tiny, almost invisible hairline crack right along one of the bottom welds. It was bleeding off all the boost pressure. I found it, I made the call on how to fix it, I ordered the parts. I can still read a complex wiring schematic, I can still mic out a crankshaft journal down to the thousandth of an inch. My mind is sharp when it comes to the work.

And at home, too, I'm still making all the decisions. I have to. If I don't decide what we're having for dinner or which bills get paid on which Friday, it doesn't happen. I'm still doing all that math, still figuring out how to stretch the last twenty dollars in my checking account until payday. 

So, no, I don't have trouble thinking clearly. It's just... like I was saying earlier, my thoughts are just hijacked by the bank. I'm not losing my focus, my focus is just being forced onto the mortgage. I'll be right in the middle of torquing down a cylinder head—which takes a lot of precision, you have to follow a very specific sequence so you don't warp the metal—and I'll do it perfectly, but the whole time, my brain is just screaming, "What if the sheriff shows up with a notice?" 

So I guess what I'm trying to say is, my brain works fine. I can make decisions just fine. I just wish I didn't have to make so many terrifying ones right now, you know? But no, no brain fog or anything like that.
Have you ever found yourself not caring about things you used to care about, even when you weren’t thinking about the financial situation?

Not caring? No... no, I wouldn't say that at all. I still care very much about everything I always have. It's not like I've just given up on life or lost interest in who I am. 

Take my kids, for instance. I still care just as much about my youngest’s spelling tests and my oldest’s softball games. My daughter is a pitcher, and she's got this wicked fastpitch that we’ve been working on since she was in grade school. Last weekend, she had a tournament out at the county complex, and I was right there in the bleachers. I still *want* to be there. I still care deeply about her ERA and whether she makes varsity next year. I was cheering for her just like I always do. It’s just that... while I'm sitting there on those cold aluminum bleachers, trying to watch her wind up, my mind keeps drifting back to that escrow shortage and the letters from the bank. 

And it's the same with my own stuff, too. I’ve got this old ’85 Chevy K10 square body truck that I’ve been slowly rebuilding in the garage for the last three years. It’s my pride and joy, really. I spent months—I mean literally months—just sourcing the correct original instrument cluster for the dash, calling scrap yards all over the tri-state area on my lunch breaks. I still love that truck. I still care about getting the timing dialed in perfectly and getting the rust sanded out of the rocker panels. 

But lately, when I go out to the garage on a Sunday afternoon and pick up a socket wrench to work on it, I just look at the truck and think, "What's the point of fixing this up if the bank takes the garage it's parked in?" 

So, if you're asking if I just stopped caring about things... no. Absolutely not. The caring is definitely still there. If you magically took this whole mortgage nightmare away today, if someone just handed me a piece of paper saying the house is safe and the taxes are paid, I’d be out in the driveway turning wrenches on that Chevy and screaming my head off at the softball game without a single worry in the world. I haven't lost who I am or what I love. I'm just so buried under all this terror about losing our home that it casts a shadow over everything else. But I definitely haven't stopped caring.
Do you find that your mind often jumps from one worry to another, even about small or everyday things, not just the financial situation?

Jumping from one worry to another? Like... little everyday things? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I don't really have that kind of brain, you know? 

Like, some people—my sister, for instance—she worries about absolutely everything. She worries if it's going to rain and ruin her weekend, she worries if she said the wrong thing to the mailman, she worries if her dog ate a weird bug in the yard. She’s just a bundle of nerves about the smallest stuff. But that's never been me. 

I'm a mechanic. My whole life, my whole career, is built on looking at a problem, diagnosing it, and fixing it one step at a time. So with everyday stuff, I just handle it. Like, just this past Tuesday, our washing machine started making this awful, high-pitched squealing and grinding noise right in the middle of the spin cycle. Now, somebody else might start panicking, worrying about how they're going to wash the kids' school clothes, worrying about water leaking all over the floor and ruining the drywall. Not me. I didn't sit there and worry about it. I just unplugged the machine, pulled off the back metal panel, and took a look. Sure enough, the main drive belt was completely frayed and slipping off the motor pulley. I just grabbed my phone, found the exact part number, and ordered a twelve-dollar replacement belt. It got here yesterday, I slapped it on, and boom, problem solved. I didn't spend one single second agonizing over it. 

And it's the same with other normal daily stuff. I don't stress about hitting traffic on the way to the depot in the mornings, or whether the foreman is going to be in a foul mood because the regional manager is coming by. I just put my steel-toe boots on, put my head down, and do the work. I don't have a hundred little worries buzzing around in my head like bees. 

It's really just the one thing. My mind doesn't bounce around from topic to topic. It's actually the exact opposite. It's more like... my brain is a heavy rig stuck in deep mud, just spinning its tires in the exact same rut, over and over and over again. And that rut is the house. The mortgage. The escrow shortage. That's it. My mind doesn't jump to worrying about what we're having for dinner, or if I remembered to pay the electric bill. I know I paid the electric bill because I have the confirmation number written down in my ledger in black ink. 

So, no, I don't worry about the small stuff. The small stuff is easy, because the small stuff makes sense. It's just this one massive, terrifying boulder sitting on my chest, and it never, ever moves.
When you're not actively thinking about the financial situation, do you still find yourself feeling anxious or worried about other events or possibilities in your life?

Anxious about other things? I mean... no. Not at all. It's kind of like what I was just saying about the washing machine, you know? I just don't have that kind of generalized fear about life. 

If I'm not thinking about the bank—which, to be honest, is rare these days—but if I'm actually distracted by something else, I feel completely normal. I don't sit around chewing my fingernails over what *might* happen tomorrow. Let me give you an example. Just last week, we had a pretty serious situation at the shop. One of the newer guys was bringing in a CAT 980M wheel loader, a massive piece of equipment, and one of the main hydraulic lines for the lift cylinder blew. I mean, it just ruptured. High-pressure hydraulic fluid was spraying absolutely everywhere, coating the bay walls, slicking up the entire concrete floor. 

Now, that is a situation where a lot of people would panic. It's incredibly dangerous. If that high-pressure fluid hits your skin, it can actually inject right into your bloodstream, which is a massive medical emergency. Plus, the floor was basically an ice rink, so you've got a huge slip-and-fall hazard. Did I get anxious? Did my heart start pounding out of my chest? No. I didn't even blink. I just yelled at the kid to kill the engine, I hit the emergency shop shutoff, and I went straight for the spill kit. I hauled over the big fifty-gallon drum of absorbent, started laying down the containment booms so it wouldn't reach the floor drains, and just took control of the situation. Once it was safe, I locked out the machine, bled the residual pressure from the accumulators, and started pulling the line off to get a replacement made. 

I didn't go home that night and lay in bed worrying, "Oh my god, what if another hydraulic line blows tomorrow? What if someone gets hurt next time?" I didn't feel any anxiety about it whatsoever. It happened, I handled it, and it was over. 

And it's like that with everything else in my life. I don't worry about my health, I don't worry about getting in a car crash on the highway, I don't worry about the kids getting into trouble. I just... deal with life as it comes. I'm a mechanic. I diagnose, I fix, I move on to the next ticket. 

It is literally *just* the house. That is the only thing that makes my stomach drop. Because with a blown hydraulic line, I know exactly which wrenches to grab and how to clean it up. But with this escrow shortage and the foreclosure notices... I don't have a tool in my box for that. I can't fix it with my own two hands, and that makes me feel completely helpless. So, no, I don't have any other worries buzzing around in the background. If you took the mortgage company out of the picture today, I'd be sleeping like a baby tonight. It's just that one, single, giant weight crushing down on me.
Do you ever find yourself feeling anxious or worried even when everything in your life seems to be going smoothly, not tied to any specific problem or stressor?

No, no, definitely not. I think... well, I feel like we might be circling the same drain here a little bit, Doc, because it really just goes back to what I was saying before. I don't just invent things to worry about out of thin air. If things are smooth, I'm smooth. 

Like, I work with this guy, Dave, one of the other diesel techs at the shop. Dave is the kind of guy who actually gets nervous when things are going *too* well, you know? Like, if we have a slow Friday afternoon, all the rigs are out of the bays, the floor is swept, and the foreman is just chilling in his office... Dave will start pacing. He'll be checking his phone, looking out the roll-up doors, muttering about how it's "too quiet" and wondering if the company is going to lay us off or if corporate is about to pull up for a surprise inspection. He literally can't handle peace and quiet. He thinks the other shoe is always about to drop.

But me? If the board is clear and the work is done, I am perfectly happy. I'll just pull up a rolling stool, grab my old Stanley thermos—the same beat-up green one I’ve been carrying around since I was taking night classes at the community college back in my twenties—and I'll pour myself a cup of coffee and just sit there. I'll watch the dust motes floating in the sunlight coming through the open bay doors, completely at peace. I don't sit there thinking, "Oh no, what if my truck's transmission goes out on the way home?" or "What if the kids get sick?" I just don't have that bug in my brain that makes me look for trouble when there isn't any. 

So, if everything in my life was actually going smoothly right now? I wouldn't be anxious at all. I'd be perfectly fine. I'd be enjoying my life and my family. The problem is just that things *aren't* smooth. There is a massive, glaring red warning light flashing on my dashboard right now, and it's this mortgage situation. If you could somehow just reach in and snip the wire to that warning light—if the bank backed off and the house was safe—I'd go right back to being the woman sitting on the stool drinking her coffee without a single care in the world. I don't manufacture worry. It has to be a real, physical threat staring me right in the face for me to feel like this.
Have you ever felt down or lost interest in life in general, even when there were no obvious problems or stressors happening at all?

Down? Like, just sad out of the blue? No. No, definitely not. I feel like... well, honestly Doc, I feel like we're kind of beating a dead horse here with this line of questioning, because it really all comes back to the exact same thing. I am a very cause-and-effect kind of person. If there's no problem, there's no bad feeling. I don't just lose interest in things for the heck of it. 

I mean, look at how I spend my free time. Or, well, how I *used* to spend it before all this started. When I'm not at the shop, I love rebuilding old carburetors. I've got this little workbench set up in my garage—it's nothing fancy, just a heavy piece of three-quarter-inch plywood bolted over a couple of steel sawhorses, but it does the trick. I can sit out there for hours with a can of carb cleaner, a set of picks, and a brass wire brush, just getting all the varnish and gunk out of the jets and the float bowls. It's incredibly satisfying work. And before this whole escrow nightmare, I was out there almost every single weekend. I loved it. I never once woke up on a Saturday morning, looked at a perfectly good day where all my bills were paid and everyone was healthy, and thought, "Gee, I just don't see the point in getting out of bed." That just isn't how my brain operates. 

If things are good, I'm good. Take last summer, for example. We took a long weekend and drove up to the state park. I had just put a new set of heavy-duty leaf springs on the truck the week before, so she was towing our little pop-up camper like an absolute dream, no sagging in the rear at all. We got up to the campsite, got the awning set up, got a fire going in the fire ring... and I was in heaven. I wasn't sitting in my folding chair staring into the woods feeling empty or sad or disconnected. I was drinking a cold beer, eating a slightly burnt hot dog, and loving every single second of my life. 

So, no, I don't get down when there's nothing wrong. I don't have that thing where people just get depressed for no reason. I'm only feeling like this right now because there is a massive, life-altering problem staring me right in the face. My house—the literal roof over my family's head—is on the line. That's a real, tangible disaster. If you took that disaster away tomorrow, I'd be right back out in the garage with my wire brush, happy as a clam. I don't invent misery when there isn't any.
Have you ever felt down or lost interest in life in general, even when there were no obvious problems or stressors happening at all?

Doc, I... didn't you literally just ask me that? I feel like we're just spinning our tires in the mud here. Like I was just saying about the carburetors and the camping trip, no. I don't get sad out of nowhere. I know you probably have a standard checklist of questions you have to get through, but I really don't know how else to say it. If my life is fine, I am fine. I don't lose interest in things. 

If you want another example, I mean, look at my Sunday mornings before this whole mortgage thing blew up in my face. I'm usually the first one out of bed. Jumping from one worry to another? Like... little everyday things? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I don't really have that kind of brain, you know? 

Like, some people—my sister, for instance—she worries about absolutely everything. She worries if it's going to rain and ruin her weekend, she worries if she said the wrong thing to the mailman, she worries if her dog ate a weird bug in the yard. Like, just this past Tuesday, our washing machine started making this awful, high-pitched squealing and grinding noise right in the middle of the spin cycle. Now, somebody else might start panicking, worrying about how they're going to wash the kids' school clothes, worrying about water leaking all over the floor and ruining the drywall. Not me. I didn't sit there and worry about it. I just unplugged the machine, pulled off the back metal panel, and took a look. Sure enough, the main drive belt was completely frayed and slipping off the motor pulley. I just grabbed my phone, found the exact part number, and ordered a twelve-dollar replacement belt. It got here yesterday, I slapped it on, and boom, problem solved. I didn't spend one single second agonizing over it. 

And it's the same with other normal daily stuff. I don't stress about hitting traffic on the way to the depot in the mornings, or whether the foreman is going to be in a foul mood because the regional manager is coming by. I just put my steel-toe boots on, put my head down, and do the work. I don't have a hundred little worries buzzing around in my head like bees. 

It's really just the one thing. My mind doesn't bounce around from topic to topic. It's actually the exact opposite. It's more like... my brain is a heavy rig stuck in deep mud, just spinning its tires in the exact same rut, over and over and over again. And that rut is the house. The mortgage. The escrow shortage. That's it. My mind doesn't jump to worrying about what we're having for dinner, or if I remembered to pay the electric bill. I know I paid the electric bill because I have the confirmation number written down in my ledger in black ink. 

So, no, I don't worry about the small stuff. The small stuff is easy, because the small stuff makes sense. It's just this one massive, terrifying boulder sitting on my chest, and it never, ever moves.

patient.answer:
Anxious about other things? I mean... no. Not at all. It's kind of like what I was just saying about the washing machine, you know? I just don't have that kind of generalized fear about life. 

If I'm not thinking about the bank—which, to be honest, is rare these days—but if I'm actually distracted by something else, I feel completely normal. I don't sit around chewing my fingernails over what *might* happen tomorrow. Let me give you an example. Just last week, we had a pretty serious situation at the shop. One of the newer guys was bringing in a CAT 980M wheel loader, a massive piece of equipment, and one of the main hydraulic lines for the lift cylinder blew. I mean, it just ruptured. High-pressure hydraulic fluid was spraying absolutely everywhere, coating the bay walls, slicking up the entire concrete floor. 

Now, that is a situation where a lot of people would panic. It's incredibly dangerous. If that high-pressure fluid hits your skin, it can actually inject right into your bloodstream, which is a massive medical emergency. Plus, the floor was basically an ice rink, so you've got a huge slip-and-fall hazard. Did I get anxious? Did my heart start pounding out of my chest? No. I didn't even blink. I just yelled at the kid to kill the engine, I hit the emergency shop shutoff, and I went straight for the spill kit. I hauled over the big fifty-gallon drum of absorbent, started laying down the containment booms so it wouldn't reach the floor drains, and just took control of the situation. Once it was safe, I locked out the machine, bled the residual pressure from the accumulators, and started pulling the line off to get a replacement made. 

I didn't go home that night and lay in bed worrying, "Oh my god, what if another hydraulic line blows tomorrow? What if someone gets hurt next time?" I didn't feel any anxiety about it whatsoever. It happened, I handled it, and it was over. 

And it's like that with everything else in my life. I don't worry about my health, I don't worry about getting in a car crash on the highway, I don't worry about the kids getting into trouble. I just... deal with life as it comes. I'm a mechanic. I diagnose, I fix, I move on to the next ticket. 

It is literally *just* the house. That is the only thing that makes my stomach drop. Because with a blown hydraulic line, I know exactly which wrenches to grab and how to clean it up. But with this escrow shortage and the foreclosure notices... I don't have a tool in my box for that. I can't fix it with my own two hands, and that makes me feel completely helpless. So, no, I don't have any other worries buzzing around in the background. If you took the mortgage company out of the picture today, I'd be sleeping like a baby tonight. It's just that one, single, giant weight crushing down on me.

He'll be checking his phone, looking out the roll-up doors, muttering about how it's "too quiet" and wondering if the company is going to lay us off or if corporate is about to pull up for a surprise inspection. I'll watch the dust motes floating in the sunlight coming through the open bay doors, completely at peace. I don't sit there thinking, "Oh no, what if my truck's transmission goes out on the way home?" or "What if the kids get sick?" I just don't have that bug in my brain that makes me look for trouble when there isn't any. 

So, if everything in my life was actually going smoothly right now? I wouldn't be anxious at all. I'd be perfectly fine. I'd be enjoying my life and my family. The problem is just that things *aren't* smooth. There is a massive, glaring red warning light flashing on my dashboard right now, and it's this mortgage situation. If you could somehow just reach in and snip the wire to that warning light—if the bank backed off and the house was safe—I'd go right back to being the woman sitting on the stool drinking her coffee without a single care in the world. I don't manufacture worry. It has to be a real, physical threat staring me right in the face for me to feel like this.
